rv.q: In general, the balance of light and dark in this very dark play does not yet feel natural.
There’s no doubt that casting a Black actor as Willy Loman (for the first time on Broadway, no less) adds a deeper dimension to this monumental role.
The blazing new Broadway revival of Arthur Miller's 'Death of a Salesman' deserves celebrating for the searching brilliance of its acting.

Alongside the virile actors playing their disappointing sons, Biff (Khris Davis) and Happy (McKinley Belcher III), Clarke and Pierce set a humble Brooklyn abode to quaking with all the disquieting power of shifting tectonic plates.
Death of a Salesman will rightly be measured against the ambitions and achievements of the play's stunning new Broadway revival

Missteps aside, this Death of a Salesman offers up a vital, fresh take on an American classic, making it all the more American for its inclusiveness, and as classic as the towering performances of Wendell Pierce and Sharon D Clarke.
Not a lick of Miller’s script has been altered, and yet, we’re given reams of new subtext about the anxiety, trauma, stress and stakes at hand.
In fact, it’s the inside of most of our heads and we have to recognize our own regrets; the vision of the past presented here feels pretentious, weirdly cinematic and, well, alienating.
Thanks to Clarke’s heartbreaking brilliance, the role of Linda is finally given her due.
None of these add-ons refresh or galvanize the story — they sedate it like theatrical Xanax.

Willy Loman’s middle-class tragedy was as powerful as ever, proving the steely endurability of Arthur Miller’s timeless rendering of the hollow American Dream. Willy has nothing but illusions of fame and wealth as he ends his selling career with no savings and an uncrossable emotional gulf between him and his alienated sons Biff and Happy.
This is why we go to the theater.
All in all, you are unlikely ever to see a finer production of Death of a Salesman than this one.

Of course, Linda's efforts are just as doomed as Willy's pursuits, and Clarke's layered performance recasts Death of a Salesman as a dual tragedy, with Linda as a hidden crux of the show to whom attention must truly be paid.
Nevertheless, this Salesman is a production for the ages, and one I cannot recommend enough.

The performances are individualized and powerful, including Pierce's mercurial Willy (jovial and hammy, then innocently bewildered and shaking), Clarke's tough-as-nails, weathered Linda (whose handling of the 'attention must be paid' monologue is superb), Khris Davis' soft and sensitive Biff, and McKinley Belcher III's oily and upbeat Happy.
Maybe the enduring message of this production is that these themes are universal, that we all suffer the same under the yolk of The American Dream.
This is a production that honors Miller's masterpiece while finding fresh insights in its familiar rhythms.
It will compel your attention, and your conscience, throughout.
If seeing previous productions of Death of a Salesman has inured you to Willy’s ultimate fate, this one should bring back the tears, and Clarke deserves a lot of credit for that difficult gift.

Nearly 75 years after it first premiered, Death of a Salesman still says more than we care to admit about America, about how one can work their entire life and end up with nothing, how you're worth more dead than you are alive, how the system is rigged against the little guy. Maybe the enduring mess...

All of Willy’s joyous American Dream jingoism is odd to hear coming from a Willy Loman who’s African American, and the genius of Pierce’s performance is how he uses that optimism to highlight the character’s self-deception.
For all the male sound and fury, this Death of a Salesman feels really, and rightly, all about her.

Unlike most other productions, this Linda sings; and in the final moment we are left with just Linda and her song in a downstage spotlight — an image more wrenching than anything you're likely to witness on Broadway this season.

Everything in the production seems pitched over the top, including Willy’s declining mental condition, which here feels more like full-blown dementia than merely a man defeated by life who is losing his grip.
But this Salesman seems not to have weathered the three years so well, losing a substantial slice of effectiveness on its journey from the Thames to the Hudson.

Pierce overplays Willy’s almost-constant anger – at life, at Linda, at his “disappointing” sons, Biff (Khris Davis) and Happy (an almost too-charismatic McKinley Belcher III) – making him less-than-sympathetic and, at times, almost insufferable.
The best thing about Miranda Cromwell's sometimes uncertain production is the opportunity it gives four lead actors to do strong, stunning, and, in some cases, highly original work.
Whether it’s the right casting, aside from the peerless Clarke in stand-by-your-man mode, is another matter entirely.
But for all the boldness of the reimagining, and the stellar track record of so much of the cast, “Death of a Salesman” is a disappointment in several ways.

It really is a wonder that Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman has never felt so alive and desperate, thanks to director Cromwell, unpacking layers upon layers of social commentary on the Black Person’s lived experience in America.
Whether Death of a Salesman is a text you’ve chewed through many times over or something you’re exposed to for the first time, this is an eye-opening revival.
In those moments, the cast rises to the occasion and this Death of a Salesman play truly soars.
In the play’s final moments, Clarke delivers a poignant requiem — the Great Migration poignantly distilled down to a moment that is at once full of mourning and survival.
Race adds another dimension to this new version of the “Death of A Salesman,” a subtext while enhancing the bigger message.
But the real cancer of this revival are the performances.

cn.t: Pierce and Clarke deliver powerful performances in this revelatory revival that casts the Lomans as Black, adding resonant new layers to Miller's classic. Though some find the staging's artistic choices distracting, most agree the production enriches the American Dream tragedy.

sg.ra: SeatPlan, TickPick and Headout all converge: center rows D-K sit at a perfect distance to take in the whole stage without craning. Row A is called out as too close for comfortable viewing. Dress Circle overhangs at Orchestra row L and the Mezz overhang only becomes obvious at row R without significantly cutting the stage, so the middle band is protected. 2017 ATG restoration upgraded legroom throughout.

SeatPlan flags Dress Circle A-B center as offering unobstructed sightlines and the 'front few rows of the Center Dress Circle' as premium; rows D-F center are repeatedly called out as great-value seats with full sweep of the stage. The 258-seat section has a good rake and generous legroom. Balcony overhang only becomes obvious at row J and doesn't cut into the stage, so every row is usable.

SeatPlan describes Balcony rows A-B center as hanging close enough for detailed views and reports sightlines 'better than average' for a third level. Rear rows G-H are the cheapest in the house. Rake is very good, but legroom is tighter than the rest of the theater and the top of the stage may be cut by the balcony's angle. AVFMS user at G110 noted that some in-audience action isn't visible from rear balcony.
